name: Dacian
confidence_why: Dacian is known only from glosses and names; the one work that touches its stress, Georgiev 1977, gives initial stress for a single word (κινούβοιλα, inferred from its Lithuanian cognate and vowel reduction) while his own Daco-Mysian sound laws assume unstressed initial vowels were lost, so no placement rule exists on record, and Duridanov 1985, Russu 1967, Katičić 1976 and Sowa 2020 are silent.

new_statements.quote: Тракийската дума din-upula и диал. sin-upyla с k' > s или þ > d (озвучено в началото на думата пред гласна), a > ə > i или u (y) в неударено положение и изместване на съгласните (b > p) съответствува точно на дакийската и литовската дума. Ударението на тракийската и дакийската дума е било на първата сричка, както в литовски, поради което следващите гласни са били редуцирани.
new_statements.translation: The Thracian word din-upula and dial. sin-upyla, with k' > s or þ > d (voiced word-initially before a vowel), a > ə > i or u (y) in unstressed position, and displacement of the consonants (b > p), corresponds exactly to the Dacian and the Lithuanian word. The stress of the Thracian and the Dacian word was on the first syllable, as in Lithuanian, which is why the following vowels were reduced.
new_statements.citation: Георгиев, Владимир И. 1977. Траките и техният език. София: Издателство на БАН, p. 14 (entry dinupula, sinupyla / Dacian κινούβοιλα)

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (page scan, printed page number 14 visible at foot) and the Bulgarian-model the scanned texthits "Ударението"). The sentence is on the page verbatim, at the end of the dinupula/sinupyla entry: "Ударението на тракийската и дакийската дума е било на първата сричка, както в литовски, поради което следващите гласни са били редуцирани.³" Minor differences from the reported quote: the page reads "a > ə > i и ŏ > u (y) в неударено положение" (the report has "a > ə > i или u (y)"), and footnote superscripts ² and ³ are omitted. Translation in the report is accurate. Footnote 3 on the same page adds only a metathesis derivation (*þ/šunipula- < *þ/šu-nēpōla- <…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Georgiev infers initial (first-syllable) stress for one Dacian lexeme, κινούβοιλα 'bryony' (< *kun-abolo-, cf. Lith. šun-obuolas), from the reduction of its post-initial vowels and from the Lithuanian cognate. He gives no general rule for Dacian stress placement; elsewhere he only presupposes a stress accent (o > u and e > i in unstressed syllables, p. 195, 197; loss of initial pretonic a-, p. 205 = 1981: 134; IE r̥, n̥ > ri, a 'under stress', p. 209 = 1981: 135).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement concerns a single word and is a reconstruction from vowel reduction plus the Lithuanian comparison.
new_statements.domain_note: Single lexeme (a Dioscorides plant name), not the language as a whole; Dacian is attested only in glosses, plant names and onomastics, so any accent statement is reconstructive. 'fixed: initial syllable' here is the reading of that one claim, not a documented word-stress system.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes 'Daco-Mysian' (дако-мизийски), Georgiev's cover term for Dacian + Moesian (Getic); Glottolog treats Dacian as daci1234. The statement's lexeme κινούβοιλα is a Dacian plant name from Dioscorides; its Thracian/Bessian counterpart dinupula belongs to Thracian (thra1250).

sources.note: p. 14 (dinupula/κινούβοιλα entry): the stress of the Thracian and the Dacian word was on the first syllable, as in Lithuanian, hence reduction of the following vowels — a single-lexeme claim. Elsewhere only presupposes a stress accent: Dac. o (< IE a) > u in unstressed syllable as in Romanian (p. 195); loss of initial unstressed/pretonic a as in Albanian and Romanian (p. 205); IE r̥, n̥ > Dac./Alb. ri, a 'под ударение' (p. 209); 'probably au > a in unstressed syllable, au > e under stress' (p. 208 n. 3). No general rule of stress placement.
Nothing on Dacian; for Thracian only 'a reduction of final unaccented /o/'.

sources.citation: Georgiev, Vladimir I. 1981. Introduction to the History of the Indo-European Languages. Sofia: Bulgarian Academy of Sciences. sec. 4.6.1 'The Comparative-Historical Phonology of Daco-Mysian and Albanian', pp. 133-135
sources.note: 'There is aphaeresis of initial protonic a (from IE a, ā, o) exactly as in Albanian and Rumanian (Dacian substratum)' (p. 134); 'IE (stressed) e shifts in Albanian into je'; 'IE r̥ > Dac., Alb. ri (stressed)', 'IE n̥ > Dac., Alb. a (stressed)' (p. 135). Presupposes stress; the κινούβοιλα entry (p. 122) does not repeat the 1977 initial-stress remark. No placement rule.

sources.note: StressTyp-based survey of European word-accent systems; in the Indo-European overview (sec. 4, p. 433) it lists Dacian among extinct branches known 'only from few inscriptions or names and glosses' and states that no reliable accentual information (stress, pitch accent or tone alike) is available or even obtainable for these languages. No tone or accent facts are given for Dacian; the work is a first-hand typologist's classification that the prosody is undeterminable.

tone.quote: Other potential branches (mostly all represented by one extinct language) are Phrygian, Venetic (possibly a form of Italic, often including Liburnian), Lusitanian, Thracian, Macedonian, Paionian, Dacian, Illyrian and Messapian (likely to be a form of Illyrian) (Beekes 1995: 17–30). The first three are known from a fair number of inscriptions, the latter four only from few inscriptions or names and glosses. Baldi (1983: 165 ff.) mentions a few other candidate IE languages known from very meager evidence (place names etc.): Ligurian, Lepontic (possibly a continental Celtic language), Sicel (close to Italic), Raetic (almost no evidence at all). No reliable accentual information is available, or even possible for these languages.
